parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a broadband company to arrange the installation of a home internet connection.
script: Good morning, Kestrel Broadband, Dana speaking. How can I help you?
Hi there. I'd like to get a new broadband connection at my house. I've just moved in and there's nothing set up.
Congratulations on the new home. I can take your order now if you like. Could I start with your surname?
Lovely, thank you, Mr Lindqvist. And what's the address where the service will be installed?
It's 38 Fennel Close. Fennel is F-E-N-N-E-L, and then Close, like closing a door.
38 Fennel Close. Is that in Bristol?
Yes, that's right, in the Horfield area.
It's BS7 3HY. Actually, hold on, let me check the letter I got from the council. Yes, BS7 3HY. For a second I thought it ended in H-Z.
No problem. BS7 3HY it is. Now, what's the best number to reach you on? We'll send a text message when the engineer is on the way.
Well, I can give you my old landline, 0117 496 2210, but I've not had calls forwarded yet, so please use my mobile. That's 07912 640 385.
07912 640 385. Perfect. Now, let's talk about the package. We have three speeds at the moment. The basic one is 75 megabits per second, then there's 150, and the top one is 300.
Hmm. What would the 300 be like for a household of three? My wife and I both work from home, and our son is always gaming.
To be honest, 300 would be more than most families use. A lot of our customers in your situation are very happy with 150. It handles several video calls at the same time without any trouble.
Then I'll go for 150. It's not worth paying for the extra speed.

Good choice. The normal price for that package is 32 pounds a month, but there's an online offer at the moment, so you'll get 4 pounds 50 off for the first twelve months. So that comes to 27 pounds 50 a month.
27 pounds 50. That's cheaper than I expected. Is there a setup fee?
No, installation is free. We do need an engineer to visit, because there's no line into the house yet. When would suit you?
I was hoping for Tuesday, if that's possible, as I'm working from home that day.
Let me see. Tuesday is fully booked, I'm afraid, and so is Wednesday. The first day I have is Thursday.
Thursday is fine, actually. I can swap my working days.
Great. We have two time slots. The morning one runs from 9 to 1, and the afternoon one from 1.30 to 5.30.
Hmm, I have a meeting on Thursday morning, so the afternoon would be better.
Then I'll put you down for 1.30. The engineer will phone you about half an hour before he arrives, so there's no need to wait around by the door.
That's very helpful. Does the package include a router?

Yes, you'll receive our latest router in the post before the visit, and since you've chosen 150, we're also giving away a free wi-fi extender. Normally those cost 40 pounds. It's useful if your home office is far from the router.
Oh, brilliant. The study is right at the top of the house, so that will help.
One last thing. Someone over eighteen has to be at home for the whole visit, and they'll need to show a passport for our records. A driving licence isn't enough, I'm afraid.
That's no problem. I'll make sure my wife has hers out.
Excellent. I'll send you a confirmation email within the hour. Is there anything else I can help with?
No, I think that's everything. Thanks very much, Dana.
You're welcome, Mr Lindqvist. Have a lovely day.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide describes the layout of a science museum to visitors at the start of a tour.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Halden Science Museum. My name's Ewan, and I'll be taking you around for the next hour. Before we start, let me give you a quick picture of how the building is laid out, because it can be a little confusing on a first visit.

We're standing in the main entrance hall on the ground floor. If you look to your left, in the west wing, you'll see the museum shop. Many people leave it until the end of the day, but I'd say go and have a look now, because the souvenir guide book is half price this week for anyone who buys it before 11 o'clock.

Now, the lockers. A lot of people ask me where they are. They used to be right here beside the shop, but they've been moved. You'll find the lockers and the cloakroom in the basement, down the stairs behind the information desk. They take one pound coins, which you get back, so it's worth leaving your coats and large bags there, particularly if you've brought rucksacks.

On the east side of this floor you can see the glass wall of the Robotics Workshop. That's where you'll find the machines that you can programme yourself. It's very popular, so if you want to take part, put your name down on the screen by the door.

Moving up, the first floor is home to the Human Body Gallery and the Electricity Hall. I should mention that the Electricity Hall is closed at the moment. We're not repairing anything, though. We're installing a brand new set of interactive displays, and it should reopen in the spring. So you'll be able to visit the Human Body Gallery, but not the Electricity Hall, I'm afraid.

The second floor is where you'll find the Skyline Café. It has a great view over the river and does hot meals until 3 o'clock. It used to be in the basement, but it's far nicer now. If the weather's good, you can take your drink out onto the terrace.

Now, the thing most people come for, the planetarium. It's the big silver dome at the very top of the building, so you take the lift to the top floor and it's right in front of you. Shows last 30 minutes.

This week we also have a special exhibition called Deep Ocean. Unlike the rest of the museum, you need a timed ticket for that, and you can get one from the information desk on the day. Tickets used to be sold online only, but we changed that last month. There's no charge for visitors under sixteen, and everyone else pays 4 pounds.

Let me say a word about the children's activities. We run hands-on workshops, which are free. At weekends there are sessions in the morning and afternoon, and on school days there's just one at 4 o'clock after the day's group visits. But during the school holidays, they run every day, with new topics each week.

The quietest times? The busiest part of the day is from about 11 to 1, when school groups arrive. Most of them have gone by 1.30, so my advice for the Space Hall, which is the most crowded gallery, is to go in the early afternoon, once the groups have left. Late afternoon tends to fill up again with families, so I wouldn't leave it until then.

A word on access. All floors have step-free access by lift. Wheelchairs can be borrowed free of charge from the information desk, and we have a quiet room on the first floor for anyone who needs a break from the noise.

Finally, a few practical points. Photography is fine everywhere except the planetarium. Please don't touch the exhibits unless they have a green button beside them. And if you get lost, just look for a member of staff in a blue shirt.

So, we'll go and look at the Space Hall first, followed by the Robotics Workshop. When our tour finishes, I'll ask you to come back to the information desk, where you can collect your belongings from the basement later or ask any questions. I hope you enjoy your visit. Now, if you'd like to follow me this way, we'll start in the Space Hall.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two nursing students, Imogen and Rhys, prepare a presentation on hand hygiene.
script: Hi, Rhys. Thanks for coming in early. I thought we should sort out our hand hygiene presentation properly today.
No problem. I've brought my laptop, so we can go through the slides together.
Great. Before we start, I've been wondering, why did we pick this topic again? I seem to remember Dr Marsh suggesting it.

She gave us a list of options, but I think we chose it ourselves. It was because of my placement on the surgical ward. I kept seeing visitors walk straight in without using the gel, and it made me realise how much depends on something so simple.

Right, that's what I remembered. Anyway, I've done most of the research. I found a good set of figures on infection rates, but I'm a bit worried. The survey only covered twelve hospitals, so I'm not sure it tells us very much.
Twelve? That is small. A national study would carry more weight. Though the results are quite striking, aren't they?
They are, but I think we should say clearly that the sample was too small to be reliable. Otherwise someone will ask about it.
Agreed. Let's mention it in the notes under the slide. Now, I sent Dr Marsh our draft last week. Did she reply?
Yes, this morning. She liked the structure, but she said the whole thing was too long. We have only fifteen minutes, and the draft would take about twenty.
Hmm. I thought it would be the amount of text on the slides. It looks so crowded.
She mentioned that, but as a smaller point. The main thing was the length.
Okay. So we need to cut some material. Let's go through the slides one at a time. Slide one is the introduction. At the moment it has a long paragraph. We could cut it to three bullet points.

Yes, definitely. Nobody reads a whole paragraph on a slide. Then slide two is the infection figures. We'll need to check them before we use them. One of the percentages doesn't match the original table.

I'll sort that out tonight. Slide three covers the five moments for hand hygiene, and I think a short video clip would work better than my diagram. The one the hospital trust made is only forty seconds.
I like that. And for slide four, the technique, we could use a photograph of the proper hand position. At the moment we have a drawing, and it isn't very clear.
Good idea. I can take one in the practice lab, and a classmate could be the model. Now the last slide, the conclusion. I'm not sure whether we should include recommendations.
That's a good question. I think we should check with Dr Marsh about it. She'll know what the assessors expect.
Yes, I'll email her this afternoon. Now, how should we begin? I was thinking of starting with a real case study, a patient who got an infection because of poor hygiene.
That could be powerful, but it might take too long, and we've just agreed to cut time. What about a quick quiz at the start, perhaps three questions like how long you should wash your hands for?
Hmm, that's quick, and it gets people involved. Okay, let's do the quiz. A case study could be a backup if we have time.
Now, what about the practical part? Are you nervous about it?
Not really. I've demonstrated the technique many times. What worries me is the questions at the end. If someone asks about a statistic that I don't know, I'll be completely stuck.
We'll prepare a list of likely questions. Between us we should be able to answer most of them, and if we can't, we can say we'll find out.
That would help. Right, I'll update the slides tonight and send them to you tomorrow morning.
Perfect. Let's meet again on Friday for a full practice run, with a stopwatch this time.
Deal. See you then. Oh, and thanks for doing so much of the research. I owe you a coffee.
I'll hold you to that. Right, I'd better run, I have a lecture at ten.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the origins of writing systems.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to look at one of the greatest inventions in human history: writing. Speech is very old, probably hundreds of thousands of years old, but writing is surprisingly recent. The first true writing systems appeared only about five thousand years ago, and to understand why, we need to start in the ancient land of Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq.

Most people assume that writing began as poetry or religion, perhaps as a way to record great stories. In fact, the earliest signs, from around 3,300 BC, were used for something far more ordinary. They recorded amounts of grain, along with other goods that were stored in the temples of the city of Uruk. Writing began as accounting.

Before that, people had already been keeping track of goods for thousands of years, using small clay tokens. A token in the shape of a cone might stand for a measure of grain, and a cylinder for an animal. These were kept in sealed clay balls. The problem was that you couldn't see inside without breaking the ball, so people began pressing the tokens into the surface first, and this was the first step towards signs on clay.

Over time, the signs became more abstract. At first, scribes drew them with a sharp point, but this was slow, and curved lines were difficult in wet clay. So they changed the tool. They cut a reed, and pressed its end into the soft surface, making wedge-shaped marks. We call this cuneiform, from the Latin word for wedge. It was used for nearly three thousand years, and for many languages, not only Sumerian.

Now, let's move to Egypt. Egyptian hieroglyphs appear a little later, around 3,200 BC, though some scholars argue that the two systems developed independently. What's certain is that hieroglyphs were meant to be beautiful. They covered the walls of temples and tombs. But the Egyptians also developed a quicker script for everyday use, written with ink on papyrus, a kind of paper made from a river plant.

For centuries, nobody could read hieroglyphs. The breakthrough came in 1799, when soldiers found a large slab of dark stone near the town of Rashid. It carried the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, a simplified Egyptian script, and Greek. Because scholars could read Greek, they had a key to the other two. It took more than twenty years of work before the code was finally cracked.

Let's turn to China, where the earliest known writing dates from around 1,200 BC, during the Shang dynasty. Kings wanted to ask the spirits questions, so they carved them into animal bones or into the shells of turtles. The cracks that appeared when the objects were heated were then read as answers. These oracle bones are our earliest evidence of Chinese characters.

One important feature of Chinese writing is that each character represents a syllable of the spoken language, and usually a whole idea at the same time. This is quite different from an alphabet, and it's one reason the system has lasted so long: speakers of very different dialects can read the same text.

Writing was also invented independently in the Americas. The Maya developed a rich script, with hundreds of signs, from about the third century BC. They carved it into stone monuments, but they also wrote on books made from the inner bark of fig trees, folded like a screen. Sadly, the Spanish destroyed almost all of these books, and only four survive.

Finally, I want to say something about the alphabet. A true alphabet, with a sign for each consonant, probably first appeared in Egypt or nearby around 1,800 BC, but it was the Phoenicians who made it famous. They were sailors and merchants from the coast of modern Lebanon, and their writing system was easy to learn. Because they travelled so widely, it spread around the Mediterranean, and trade was the main reason it became so common.

The final step was taken by the Greeks, around 800 BC. Phoenician writing had signs only for consonants. The Greeks borrowed it, but they used some of the extra signs they did not need for the sounds they had. This gave them letters for vowels, so for the first time every sound in the language could be shown. Our own alphabet descends directly from theirs, by way of the Romans.

To sum up, writing was not invented once, by one person. It emerged in several places, for practical reasons, and it was shaped by the materials people had to hand: clay, reeds, stone, bark and bone. Next week we'll look at how printing changed all of this. Thank you.

passages.title: Four days out from Marlow Bay
paras: Whether you are staying for a weekend or a full week, the Marlow Bay area offers days out for every taste. Here are four of our favourites, all within an hour's journey of the town centre.

A  Hollin Castle and Gardens. The ruined castle stands on a hill above the river and is open daily from April to October, except Mondays. Entry is by ticket at the gate, so there is no need to book. Visitors who are happy with heights can climb the 112 steps of the west tower for views across the whole valley. Below, the walled gardens are at their best in June. Please note that dogs are not allowed inside the castle grounds. There is a small tea room beside the main gate, and a leaflet with a map of the walks around the hill is available free of charge.

B  Saltern Island Ferry. A 45-minute crossing takes you to a quiet island famous for its seabirds and sandy beaches. The boat runs every day from May to September, but departures depend on the tide, and sailings are cancelled in rough weather. Places are limited, so booking in advance is essential; you can reserve online or at the harbour office. Dogs cannot be taken on the ferry, with the exception of assistance dogs. Warm clothing is recommended, as the wind on the open deck can be strong even in summer.

C  Brackenridge Steam Railway. Travel through woodland and farmland in beautifully restored carriages from the 1930s. Trains operate at weekends and during school holidays, whatever the weather, and tickets can be bought at the station on the day. Under-fives travel free. Well-behaved dogs are welcome on board, and there is a small café on the platform serving tea, coffee and homemade cakes.

D  Thornfield Farm and Market. Every Saturday, the farm opens its doors to the public with a market of local food and a guided tour of the dairy, where you can watch the cheesemaker at work. Tours are held only on Saturdays and finish with a tasting of five cheeses, which is included in the tour price of 6 pounds. Parking is free, and there is no need to book. Wellington boots are advisable in wet weather, as some of the tour takes place in the farmyard.

passages.title: Ashbourne House Hotel: guest information
paras: Welcome to Ashbourne House. We hope you enjoy your stay. This sheet explains a few things that will help to make your visit more comfortable.

Breakfast. A full breakfast is served in the Conservatory from 7 am to 10 am on weekdays, and from 8 am to 11 am at weekends. If you need to leave early, please let reception know the evening before, and we will prepare a packed breakfast for you.
Wi-fi. The wi-fi password is printed on your key card holder. If you have any difficulty connecting, please call reception on extension 0.
Parking. Guests may use our car park free of charge. Please collect a parking permit from reception when you check in and display it on your windscreen. Vehicles without a permit may be removed.

Check-out. Rooms must be vacated by 11 am. If you would like to stay later, please ask at the front desk; a late check-out may be possible for a small charge, depending on availability. After you have checked out, you are welcome to leave your bags in the luggage room next to reception until the evening.

Laundry. Place your clothes in the bag provided in your wardrobe and leave it at reception. Laundry handed in before 9 am will be returned the same day. Items handed in later are returned the following morning.

Quiet hours. To make sure all guests can rest, we ask you to keep noise to a minimum between 10 pm and 7 am. Smoking is not permitted anywhere in the hotel; there is a seating area in the garden for smokers.
Pets. Regrettably, we cannot accept pets, except for assistance dogs.
Emergencies. In an emergency, dial 9 from your room telephone. Fire exits are marked on the back of your bedroom door. Please read the instructions carefully when you arrive.

passages.title: Working at height: site safety rules
paras: A  Falls from a height remain the biggest single cause of death on construction sites, and many serious injuries happen at heights of less than two metres. That is why every person employed on a Calder & Reeve site, whether permanent staff or contractor, must follow these rules. They apply to anyone who works where they could fall, including on roofs, scaffolding, ladders, platforms and next to open edges or holes in floors.

B  Before any job at height begins, the site supervisor must complete a written risk assessment. This should include a check of the weather forecast. All work on roofs and scaffolds must stop if the wind speed rises above 23 mph, or if there is ice or heavy rain. The supervisor must also make sure that the area below the work is closed off, so that tools or materials which fall cannot injure anyone.

C  Working at height should be avoided wherever the job can be done from the ground. Where it cannot, the safest option should always be chosen. Mobile platforms and scaffold towers come first. A ladder may be used only for light work of short duration, never longer than 30 minutes in one place, and only when it is secured and the worker can keep three points of contact with it at all times. Under no circumstances should a worker carry heavy loads up a ladder.

D  All equipment must be checked by the person using it before each shift. Ladders with bent rungs, cracks or missing feet must be taken out of use at once and reported. Scaffolding is inspected every seven days by a competent person, who attaches a coloured tag at the entrance. A green tag means that it is safe to use. A red tag means that it must not be used under any circumstances until it has been repaired and inspected again.

E  Where a fall cannot be prevented by guard rails or platforms, workers must wear a safety harness fitted by a trained person. The lanyard must be short enough to stop a fall before the worker reaches the ground, and must be attached to a strong anchor point above the head if possible. Hard hats with chin straps are compulsory in all areas at height, and boots must have non-slip soles. Tools must be attached to the worker's belt or carried in a bag, so that nothing can be dropped on people below.

F  No one should work at height alone. If someone is injured, the rescue plan, which is displayed on the site notice board, must be followed. Near misses, where nobody was hurt but could have been, must be reported to the supervisor on the same day. Reports help us to learn lessons and to improve the rules, and nobody will be punished for making an honest report. All reports are reviewed by the safety manager at the monthly meeting.

passages.title: Overtime: how to claim
paras: Calder & Reeve recognises that, from time to time, our work requires staff to put in extra hours. This guide explains how overtime is approved and paid.

Who can claim. All permanent employees who work on site or in the depot are eligible for overtime pay. Overtime is any work done in addition to your contracted hours. Managers and those working under a salaried agreement are not eligible.

Approval. Overtime must always be agreed with your supervisor in advance, preferably the day before, and recorded on the daily planner. Hours worked without approval will not be paid, except in a genuine emergency, in which case you must tell your supervisor as soon as possible afterwards.

Rates of pay. The standard overtime rate for weekday evenings and Saturdays is time and a half, which is one and a half times your normal hourly rate. Work on Sundays is paid at time and a half as well. Double time is paid only for work on public holidays.

How to claim. Claims must be entered on the online timesheet system at the end of each week, and your supervisor will approve them electronically. Claims received by the 20th of the month will be included in that month's salary. Any claim submitted after that date will be paid the following month. If you have difficulty using the system, ask the office administrator for help. Paper forms are no longer accepted, and your supervisor cannot enter a claim on your behalf.
Queries. If you believe that your overtime has been calculated incorrectly, please contact the payroll team within 28 days of receiving your payslip.

passages.title: From bitter drink to sweet bar: the story of chocolate
paras: A  Chocolate begins with the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows only in the warm, wet regions close to the equator. Archaeologists believe that people in Central America were using cacao at least 3,500 years ago. The earliest chocolate was not at all like the sweet bars we know today. The seeds were roasted, ground and mixed with water, and often with chilli and ground maize, to produce a bitter, frothy drink. It was prepared for religious ceremonies and was believed to have special powers. Pots found in ancient burial sites still carry traces of the chemicals that cacao contains, which shows how highly the drink was valued. Trees were planted close to villages, and the harvest, which came twice a year, was a time of celebration. Nobody then could have imagined that the drink would one day travel across the world.

B  By the time of the Aztec empire in the fifteenth century, cacao was one of the most valuable goods in the region. The beans were used as money: records suggest that a turkey could be bought for a hundred beans, and that a rabbit cost ten. Only rulers, warriors and wealthy merchants were allowed to drink chocolate regularly. When Spanish explorers arrived in the early sixteenth century, they were offered it as a gift, but at first they found the taste unpleasant. One soldier wrote that the drink looked more suitable for pigs than for people. Yet the explorers soon noticed how much it mattered to the people they met, and some of them began to wonder whether it might be worth sending home.

C  It was the Spanish who changed chocolate. They took cacao back across the Atlantic, and began adding cane sugar, cinnamon and other spices, then served the drink hot. This sweeter version proved far more popular with European tastes than the original. For nearly a hundred years, the Spanish managed to keep the method of preparation a secret, so that chocolate remained unknown to most people elsewhere in Europe. The secret eventually spread through royal marriages, monasteries and, according to some accounts, through the pirates who raided Spanish ships. By the middle of the seventeenth century, every important court in Europe had its own chocolate maker, and elegant cups and pots were made specially for serving the drink.

D  By the seventeenth century, chocolate had become fashionable in Paris, Amsterdam and London, where special chocolate houses opened. These were places where wealthy customers gathered to drink the beverage, to talk business and to discuss politics. Few ordinary people could ever afford it, since the beans had to be shipped across the ocean, and governments added heavy taxes. Some people also claimed that chocolate could cure illness, which helped to keep the price high. For several generations, drinking chocolate in the morning was a sign of wealth, in the same way that owning a carriage or a fine house was. Cooks and doctors wrote recipes for it, and the recipes grew more elaborate every year.

E  The industrial revolution transformed the way chocolate was made. In 1828, a Dutch chemist invented a press that squeezed most of the natural fat, called cocoa butter, out of the ground beans. What was left could be crushed into a fine powder which dissolved easily in water or milk. The process made chocolate cheaper and easier to prepare. Then, in 1847, a British manufacturer discovered that, by mixing the powder with melted cocoa butter and sugar, a paste could be made that would set solid. The first chocolate bar for eating had been created. Factories soon began to make it in large numbers, driven by steam engines, and bars were wrapped and sold in shops across the country.

F  Early bars were rather coarse and gritty. In the 1870s, a Swiss manufacturer finally solved the problem of how to make a smooth, creamy product, by adding powdered milk to the mixture, which led to the world's first milk chocolate. A few years later, a colleague invented a machine called a conche, which stirred the mixture for several days. This removed the grainy texture and produced the melting quality that people expect from good chocolate today. By 1900, chocolate was no longer a luxury for the rich, but a treat that millions of people could buy. Companies competed with each other by inventing new fillings, and boxes of chocolates became popular gifts. During two world wars, chocolate was also given to soldiers because it was light, kept well and provided energy.

G  Today the world eats over seven million tonnes of chocolate a year. About seventy per cent of the world's cacao is grown in West Africa, mostly by small family farms. Many farmers earn very little, and there are serious concerns about child labour and the cutting down of forests to make room for new plantations. Several large companies have introduced certification schemes in response, but critics argue that these are not enough. Meanwhile, some small makers have returned to the old methods, buying beans directly from farmers and making the chocolate themselves. Others have started to sell dark chocolate with a very high cocoa content, and customers are now willing to pay more for it if they know where it came from. In a way, the story has come full circle, and a drink once reserved for emperors is once again being appreciated as a rare and precious thing.

items.q: What was the main effect of the press invented in 1828?
options: It improved the flavour of chocolate.

items.why: The text says the process made chocolate cheaper and easier to prepare.

items.q: What does the writer say about the conche?
options: It was invented by the maker of the first milk chocolate.
It was used to add powdered milk.
It worked more quickly than earlier machines.
It gave chocolate a smooth, melting quality.
items.why: The machine removed the grainy texture. It was invented by a colleague of the milk chocolate maker, and it stirred for days, so A and C are wrong.

Most farmers earn a high income.
Certification has solved the main problems.
It is mainly carried out in Central America.

to compare the chocolate of different countries
to describe how chocolate has changed over time
